podcast.body: MCA Records, Newton-John's American label, strategically promoted this twangy, mid-tempo song to country radio first. It debuted on the Hot Country Singles chart in August 1973 at number 97 (her first appearance on that chart), slowly climbing to number 7 just before Christmas 1973. By then the song had also debuted on the Hot 100 where it eventually reached number 6 in February 1974, becoming her first top 10 pop hit. "Let me be there in your morning. Let me be there in your life."

podcast.body: Released as a single in 1973, this song was a top 10 hit on both the country and pop charts, and earned her a Grammy for Best Country Vocal Performance. "Well, I mean we could start with Let Me Be There which was released as a single in 1973. She was a top 10 hit on both the country and pop charts."

This song was released as a single and became a significant crossover hit, reaching number six on the Billboard Hot 100 and number seven on the country chart. Its catchy beat and country-pop sound resonated with the American public during a time of national change in 1973, aligning with a desire for middle-of-the-road pop music. "Let me be there in your heart and let me be there in your mind. Let me change whatever it's for and make it blind."

Olivia Newton-John's vocals on "Let Me Be There" earned her a Grammy in 1974, a win that caused significant upset within the traditional country music industry. "She upset a lot of people in the country music industry for winning a Grammy in 1974 for her vocals for Let Me Be There."
